    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        integer & !odd  --> even

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.
    """
    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):
        # save a copy of the facts dict
        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:
            self._generator = facts.generator
        if facts:
            self.deduce_all_facts(facts)

    def copy(self):
        return self.__class__(self)

    @property
    def generator(self):
        return self._generator.copy()


def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None


class ManagedProperties(BasicMeta):
    """Metaclass for classes with old-style assumptions"""
    def __init__(cls, *args, **kws):
        BasicMeta.__init__(cls, *args, **kws)

        local_defs = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            attrname = as_property(k)
            v = cls.__dict__.get(attrname, '')
            if isinstance(v, (bool, integer_types, type(None))):
                if v is not None:
                    v = bool(v)
                local_defs[k] = v

        defs = {}
        for base in reversed(cls.__bases__):
            try:
                defs.update(base._explicit_class_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                pass
        defs.update(local_defs)

        cls._explicit_class_assumptions = defs
        cls.default_assumptions = StdFactKB(defs)

        cls._prop_handler = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            try:
                cls._prop_handler[k] = getattr(cls, '_eval_is_%s' % k)
            except AttributeError:
                pass

        # Put definite results directly into the class dict, for speed
        for k, v in cls.default_assumptions.items():
            setattr(cls, as_property(k), v)

        # protection e.g. for Integer.is_even=F <- (Rational.is_integer=F)
        derived_from_bases = set()
        for base in cls.__bases__:
            try:
                derived_from_bases |= set(base.default_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                continue  # not an assumption-aware class
        for fact in derived_from_bases - set(cls.default_assumptions):
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if pname not in cls.__dict__:
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

        # Finally, add any missing automagic property (e.g. for Basic)
        for fact in _assume_defined:
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if not hasattr(cls, pname):
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

from sympy import *

# The problematic case
expr = -2*I + (1 + I)**2
print(f"Expression: {expr}")
print(f"  is_zero: {expr.is_zero}")

# Let's manually trace through the logic
nz = []  # non-zero real parts
z = 0    # count of zero parts
im_or_z = False  # some parts that are real or zero when multiplied by I
im = False  # purely imaginary parts

for a in expr.args:
    print(f"\nArg: {a}")
    if a.is_real:
        print("  is_real")
        if a.is_zero:
            z += 1
            print(f"  -> zero, z={z}")
        elif a.is_zero is False:
            nz.append(a)
            print(f"  -> non-zero real, nz={nz}")
        else:
            print("  -> unknown real, returning None")
    elif a.is_imaginary:
        print("  is_imaginary")
        im = True
        print(f"  -> im={im}")
    elif (S.ImaginaryUnit*a).is_real:
        print("  (I*a).is_real")
        im_or_z = True
        print(f"  -> im_or_z={im_or_z}")
    else:
        print("  -> unknown type, returning None")

print(f"\nSummary:")
print(f"  z={z}, len(args)={len(expr.args)}")
print(f"  nz={nz}")
print(f"  im={im}, im_or_z={im_or_z}")

if z == len(expr.args):
    print("Result: True (all zero)")
elif len(nz) == len(expr.args):
    print("Result: None (all non-zero real)")
else:
    b = Add(*nz) if nz else S.Zero
    print(f"  b = Add(*nz) = {b}")
    print(f"  b.is_zero = {b.is_zero}")
    
    if b.is_zero:
        print("  b.is_zero is True")
        if not im_or_z and not im:
            print("  -> Result: True (no imaginary parts)")
        elif im and not im_or_z:
            print("  -> Result: False (only imaginary parts) <-- THIS IS THE BUG!")
    if b.is_zero is False:
        print("  b.is_zero is False")
        print("  -> Result: False")
    
    # The issue: we should check if the imaginary parts sum to zero too!
    if im or im_or_z:
        im_parts = [a for a in expr.args if a.is_imaginary or (I*a).is_real]
        im_sum = Add(*im_parts)
        print(f"\n  Sum of imaginary parts: {im_sum}")
        print(f"  im_sum.is_zero: {im_sum.is_zero}")
        print(f"  simplify(im_sum): {simplify(im_sum)}")
        print(f"  simplify(im_sum).is_zero: {simplify(im_sum).is_zero}")

def _eval_is_zero_fixed(self):
    """Fixed version of _eval_is_zero"""
    if self.is_commutative is False:
        return
    
    nz = []  # non-zero real parts
    z = 0    # count of zero parts
    im_or_z = False  # parts that are real or zero when multiplied by I
    im = False  # purely imaginary parts
    im_nz = []  # non-zero imaginary parts (NEW!)
    
    for a in self.args:
        if a.is_real:
            if a.is_zero:
                z += 1
            elif a.is_zero is False:
                nz.append(a)
            else:
                return
        elif a.is_imaginary:
            im = True
            if a.is_zero is False:  # NEW: track non-zero imaginary parts
                im_nz.append(a)
            elif a.is_zero is None:
                return  # NEW: if we don't know if it's zero, we can't decide
        elif (S.ImaginaryUnit*a).is_real:
            im_or_z = True
        else:

    if z == len(self.args):

    if len(nz) == len(self.args):
        return None
    
    b = self.func(*nz)
    
    if b.is_zero:

        if im and not im_or_z:

            if im_nz:

                if im_sum.is_zero is True:
                    return True
                # if im_sum.is_zero is None or False, we need more checking
                # but we should return None rather than False
            return None  # We can't be sure
    
    if b.is_zero is False:
        return False

cat > /tmp/understand_issue.txt << 'EOF'
Current logic:
- When b.is_zero (real part sum is zero) and im=True and not im_or_z (only imaginary parts), return False

Problem:
- This assumes imaginary parts can't sum to zero, which is wrong!
- Example: 2*I - 2*I = 0

Fix:
- Track non-zero imaginary parts in im_nz list
- When checking, if im and not im_or_z:
  - If im_nz is empty: all imaginary parts are zero, return True
  - If im_nz is not empty: check if im_sum.is_zero
    - If True: return True
    - If False or None: return None (can't be sure without simplification)

But wait: if im_nz has elements with is_zero=False, we still can't be sure they sum to zero
without simplification. So we should always return None in this case.

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set

    transcendental

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.

    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):

        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:
            self._generator = facts.generator
        if facts:

    def generator(self):
        return self._generator.copy()


def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None

                local_defs[k] = v

        defs = {}

            try:

            except AttributeError:

        defs.update(local_defs)

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see

    integer

        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive

        object is a real number that is not zero.

    def getit(self):

        except KeyError:

            return _ask(fact, self)

    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])

        if pk in handler_map:

            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:

    return None

            except AttributeError:

This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False

    False

implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.

This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via

have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real

implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])

        if pk in handler_map:

            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:

    return None

This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:

        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:

    return None

                local_defs[k] = v

            except AttributeError:

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see

    real
        object can have only values from the set

    integer
        object can have only values from the set

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

        object can have only values from the set

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set

    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)

        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set

    irrational

        object can have only positive (only

    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        integer & !odd  --> even

    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set
        of transcendental numbers [10]_.

    irrational
        object value cannot be represented exactly by Rational, see [5]_.

    finite
    infinite
        object absolute value is bounded (arbitrarily large).
        See [7]_, [8]_, [9]_.

    negative
    nonnegative
        object can have only negative (nonnegative)
        values [1]_.

    positive
    nonpositive
        object can have only positive (only
        nonpositive) values.

    hermitian
    antihermitian
        object belongs to the field of hermitian
        (antihermitian) operators.

def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None

        defs.update(local_defs)

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set

    irrational

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.

    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):

        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:

        if facts:

def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set
        of transcendental numbers [10]_.

    irrational
        object value cannot be represented exactly by Rational, see [5]_.

    finite
    infinite
        object absolute value is bounded (arbitrarily large).
        See [7]_, [8]_, [9]_.

    negative
    nonnegative
        object can have only negative (nonnegative)
        values [1]_.

    positive
    nonpositive
        object can have only positive (only
        nonpositive) values.

    hermitian
    antihermitian
        object belongs to the field of hermitian
        (antihermitian) operators.

Examples
========

    >>> from sympy import Symbol
    >>> x = Symbol('x', real=True); x

=====

Assumption values are stored in obj._assumptions dictionary or
are returned by getter methods (with property decorators) or are
attributes of objects/classes.

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.
    """
    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):
        # save a copy of the facts dict
        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:
            self._generator = facts.generator
        if facts:
            self.deduce_all_facts(facts)

    def copy(self):
        return self.__class__(self)

    @property
    def generator(self):
        return self._generator.copy()


def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None


class ManagedProperties(BasicMeta):
    """Metaclass for classes with old-style assumptions"""
    def __init__(cls, *args, **kws):
        BasicMeta.__init__(cls, *args, **kws)

        local_defs = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            attrname = as_property(k)
            v = cls.__dict__.get(attrname, '')
            if isinstance(v, (bool, integer_types, type(None))):
                if v is not None:
                    v = bool(v)
                local_defs[k] = v

        defs = {}
        for base in reversed(cls.__bases__):
            try:
                defs.update(base._explicit_class_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                pass
        defs.update(local_defs)

        cls._explicit_class_assumptions = defs
        cls.default_assumptions = StdFactKB(defs)

        cls._prop_handler = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            try:
                cls._prop_handler[k] = getattr(cls, '_eval_is_%s' % k)
            except AttributeError:
                pass

        # Put definite results directly into the class dict, for speed
        for k, v in cls.default_assumptions.items():
            setattr(cls, as_property(k), v)

        # protection e.g. for Integer.is_even=F <- (Rational.is_integer=F)
        derived_from_bases = set()
        for base in cls.__bases__:
            try:
                derived_from_bases |= set(base.default_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                continue  # not an assumption-aware class
        for fact in derived_from_bases - set(cls.default_assumptions):
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if pname not in cls.__dict__:
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

        # Finally, add any missing automagic property (e.g. for Basic)
        for fact in _assume_defined:
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if not hasattr(cls, pname):
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

    True

    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.
    """
    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):
        # save a copy of the facts dict
        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:
            self._generator = facts.generator
        if facts:
            self.deduce_all_facts(facts)

    def copy(self):
        return self.__class__(self)

    @property
    def generator(self):
        return self._generator.copy()


def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None


class ManagedProperties(BasicMeta):
    """Metaclass for classes with old-style assumptions"""
    def __init__(cls, *args, **kws):
        BasicMeta.__init__(cls, *args, **kws)

        local_defs = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            attrname = as_property(k)
            v = cls.__dict__.get(attrname, '')
            if isinstance(v, (bool, integer_types, type(None))):
                if v is not None:
                    v = bool(v)
                local_defs[k] = v

        defs = {}
        for base in reversed(cls.__bases__):
            try:
                defs.update(base._explicit_class_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                pass
        defs.update(local_defs)

        cls._explicit_class_assumptions = defs
        cls.default_assumptions = StdFactKB(defs)

        cls._prop_handler = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            try:
                cls._prop_handler[k] = getattr(cls, '_eval_is_%s' % k)
            except AttributeError:
                pass

        # Put definite results directly into the class dict, for speed
        for k, v in cls.default_assumptions.items():
            setattr(cls, as_property(k), v)

        # protection e.g. for Integer.is_even=F <- (Rational.is_integer=F)
        derived_from_bases = set()
        for base in cls.__bases__:
            try:
                derived_from_bases |= set(base.default_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                continue  # not an assumption-aware class
        for fact in derived_from_bases - set(cls.default_assumptions):
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if pname not in cls.__dict__:
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

        # Finally, add any missing automagic property (e.g. for Basic)
        for fact in _assume_defined:
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if not hasattr(cls, pname):
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set
        of transcendental numbers [10]_.

    irrational
        object value cannot be represented exactly by Rational, see [5]_.

    finite
    infinite
        object absolute value is bounded (arbitrarily large).
        See [7]_, [8]_, [9]_.

    negative
    nonnegative
        object can have only negative (nonnegative)
        values [1]_.

    positive
    nonpositive
        object can have only positive (only
        nonpositive) values.

    hermitian
    antihermitian
        object belongs to the field of hermitian
        (antihermitian) operators.

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.

    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):

        if not facts:

        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:

def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set
        of transcendental numbers [10]_.

    irrational
        object value cannot be represented exactly by Rational, see [5]_.

        object absolute value is bounded (arbitrarily large).

        object can have only negative (nonnegative)

    positive

        object can have only positive (only
        nonpositive) values.

    hermitian

        object belongs to the field of hermitian

    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are

    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd

        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set

    transcendental

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        integer & !odd  --> even

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with

        object can have only values from the set

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see
        `issue #7649 <https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/7649>`_.

    real
        object can have only values from the set
        of real numbers.

    integer
        object can have only values from the set
        of integers.

    odd
    even
        object can have only values from the set of
        odd (even) integers [2]_.

    prime
        object is a natural number greater than ``1`` that has
        no positive divisors other than ``1`` and itself.  See [6]_.

    composite
        object is a positive integer that has at least one positive
        divisor other than ``1`` or the number itself.  See [4]_.

    zero
        object has the value of ``0``.

    nonzero
        object is a real number that is not zero.

    rational
        object can have only values from the set
        of rationals.

    algebraic
        object can have only values from the set
        of algebraic numbers [11]_.

    transcendental
        object can have only values from the set
        of transcendental numbers [10]_.

    irrational
        object value cannot be represented exactly by Rational, see [5]_.

    finite
    infinite
        object absolute value is bounded (arbitrarily large).
        See [7]_, [8]_, [9]_.

    negative
    nonnegative
        object can have only negative (nonnegative)
        values [1]_.

    positive
    nonpositive
        object can have only positive (only
        nonpositive) values.

    hermitian
    antihermitian
        object belongs to the field of hermitian
        (antihermitian) operators.

Examples
========

    >>> from sympy import Symbol
    >>> x = Symbol('x', real=True); x
    x
    >>> x.is_real
    True
    >>> x.is_complex
    True

See Also
========

.. seealso::

    :py:class:`sympy.core.numbers.ImaginaryUnit`
    :py:class:`sympy.core.numbers.Zero`
    :py:class:`sympy.core.numbers.One`

Notes
=====

Assumption values are stored in obj._assumptions dictionary or
are returned by getter methods (with property decorators) or are
attributes of objects/classes.


References
==========

.. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_number
.. [2] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_%28mathematics%29
.. [3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imaginary_number
.. [4] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_number
.. [5] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_number
.. [6] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number

.. [10] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_number
.. [11] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_number

class StdFactKB(FactKB):
    """A FactKB specialised for the built-in rules

    This is the only kind of FactKB that Basic objects should use.
    """
    rules = _assume_rules

    def __init__(self, facts=None):
        # save a copy of the facts dict
        if not facts:
            self._generator = {}
        elif not isinstance(facts, FactKB):
            self._generator = facts.copy()
        else:
            self._generator = facts.generator
        if facts:
            self.deduce_all_facts(facts)

    def copy(self):
        return self.__class__(self)

    @property
    def generator(self):
        return self._generator.copy()


def as_property(fact):
    """Convert a fact name to the name of the corresponding property"""
    return 'is_%s' % fact


def make_property(fact):
    """Create the automagic property corresponding to a fact."""

    def getit(self):
        try:
            return self._assumptions[fact]
        except KeyError:
            if self._assumptions is self.default_assumptions:
                self._assumptions = self.default_assumptions.copy()
            return _ask(fact, self)

    getit.func_name = as_property(fact)
    return property(getit)


def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.
    """
    assumptions = obj._assumptions
    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:
        a = evaluate(obj)
        if a is not None:
            assumptions.deduce_all_facts(((fact, a),))
            return a

    # Try assumption's prerequisites
    prereq = list(_assume_rules.prereq[fact])
    shuffle(prereq)
    for pk in prereq:
        if pk in assumptions:
            continue
        if pk in handler_map:
            _ask(pk, obj)

            # we might have found the value of fact
            ret_val = assumptions.get(fact)
            if ret_val is not None:
                return ret_val

    # Note: the result has already been cached
    return None


class ManagedProperties(BasicMeta):
    """Metaclass for classes with old-style assumptions"""
    def __init__(cls, *args, **kws):
        BasicMeta.__init__(cls, *args, **kws)

        local_defs = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            attrname = as_property(k)
            v = cls.__dict__.get(attrname, '')
            if isinstance(v, (bool, integer_types, type(None))):
                if v is not None:
                    v = bool(v)
                local_defs[k] = v

        defs = {}
        for base in reversed(cls.__bases__):
            try:
                defs.update(base._explicit_class_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                pass
        defs.update(local_defs)

        cls._explicit_class_assumptions = defs
        cls.default_assumptions = StdFactKB(defs)

        cls._prop_handler = {}
        for k in _assume_defined:
            try:
                cls._prop_handler[k] = getattr(cls, '_eval_is_%s' % k)
            except AttributeError:
                pass

        # Put definite results directly into the class dict, for speed
        for k, v in cls.default_assumptions.items():
            setattr(cls, as_property(k), v)

        # protection e.g. for Integer.is_even=F <- (Rational.is_integer=F)
        derived_from_bases = set()
        for base in cls.__bases__:
            try:
                derived_from_bases |= set(base.default_assumptions)
            except AttributeError:
                continue  # not an assumption-aware class
        for fact in derived_from_bases - set(cls.default_assumptions):
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if pname not in cls.__dict__:
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

        # Finally, add any missing automagic property (e.g. for Basic)
        for fact in _assume_defined:
            pname = as_property(fact)
            if not hasattr(cls, pname):
                setattr(cls, pname, make_property(fact))

"""
This module contains the machinery handling assumptions.

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
.is_<assumption name> attribute.

Assumptions determine certain properties of symbolic objects and can
have 3 possible values: True, False, None.  True is returned if the
object has the property and False is returned if it doesn't or can't
(i.e. doesn't make sense):

    >>> from sympy import I
    >>> I.is_algebraic
    True
    >>> I.is_real
    False
    >>> I.is_prime
    False

When the property cannot be determined (or when a method is not
implemented) None will be returned, e.g. a generic symbol, x, may or
may not be positive so a value of None is returned for x.is_positive.

By default, all symbolic values are in the largest set in the given context
without specifying the property. For example, a symbol that has a property
being integer, is also real, complex, etc.

Here follows a list of possible assumption names:

.. glossary::

    commutative
        object commutes with any other object with
        respect to multiplication operation.

    complex
        object can have only values from the set
        of complex numbers.

    imaginary
        object value is a number that can be written as a real
        number multiplied by the imaginary unit ``I``.  See
        [3]_.  Please note, that ``0`` is not considered to be an
        imaginary number, see

def _ask(fact, obj):
    """
    Find the truth value for a property of an object.

    This function is called when a request is made to see what a fact
    value is.

    For this we use several techniques:

    First, the fact-evaluation function is tried, if it exists (for
    example _eval_is_integer). Then we try related facts. For example

        rational   -->   integer

    another example is joined rule:

        integer & !odd  --> even

    so in the latter case if we are looking at what 'even' value is,
    'integer' and 'odd' facts will be asked.

    In all cases, when we settle on some fact value, its implications are
    deduced, and the result is cached in ._assumptions.

    handler_map = obj._prop_handler

    # Store None into the assumptions so that recursive attempts at
    # evaluating the same fact don't trigger infinite recursion.
    assumptions._tell(fact, None)

    # First try the assumption evaluation function if it exists
    try:
        evaluate = handler_map[fact]
    except KeyError:
        pass
    else:

    return None

All symbolic objects have assumption attributes that can be accessed via
